extracted.intended_audience: legal researchers, game developers, and general readers interested in video game copyright law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles used to evaluate whether one video game infringes another's copyright, including what elements are protectable and how courts compare similarities and differences between games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea–expression distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects only the expression of an idea, not the underlying idea itself (the "idea-expression distinction" as cited from Mazer v. Stein).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will permit appropriation of broad ideas (e.g., a game about a spaceship shooting space rocks) so long as the defendant's expression is different from the plaintiff's particular expression. The page repeatedly emphasizes that taking an idea is not prohibited; only copying protectable expression is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements identified as copyrightable in a game
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge Young granted copyright protection to Atari for "the symbols that appear on the display screen, the ways in which those symbols move around the screen, and the sound emanating from the game cabinet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing infringement, courts may focus on concrete expressive elements such as on-screen symbols, their movement/animation, and sounds. Protectability turns on whether these elements are sufficiently original/particularized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scènes à faire / inevitable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that are intrinsic or inevitable to a genre or idea (scènes à faire) are not protected by copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court characterized many similarities as "inevitable" or intrinsic to the idea of shooting space rocks and thus unprotectable. Assessors should identify which similarities arise from the generic idea or functional demands of the game versus which are original expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial similarity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegation that one work is "substantially similar" to another requires comparison of protected expressive elements, not broad ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts compare similarities and differences between the works (the article notes Judge Young found 22 similar instances and nine differences) and decide whether the similarities are in protectable expression. The analysis may be both qualitative and quantitative (listing instances) and consider whether similarities are protected or unprotectable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative comparison of similarities and differences
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual method used by the court: enumerating specific instances of identical or similar features versus differences (e.g., 22 similarities and 9 differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting and describing particular similarities/differences (such as game rules, object behaviors, scoring thresholds) helps structure the court's infringement inquiry, but counts alone do not determine protectability — context and whether the items are expression or idea matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall "feel" of the game as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The court considered the games' overall "feel" (e.g., speed, difficulty, graphical realism) when concluding they were different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of overall feel is a subjective factor; commentators criticized this approach as inadequate unless the judge actually experienced playing both games. Use with caution and support with concrete expressive differences where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularized implementation may be protected
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly particularized or distinctive implementations of an idea (e.g., Pac‑Man's pie-shaped gobbler and ghosts) can be copyrightable as specific expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare whether disputed elements are generic or are distinctive, specialized expressive choices; the more particularized and original the element, the greater the likelihood of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/standardized game mechanics are less likely protectable
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional features or mechanics (e.g., three sizes of rocks that split into two smaller rocks, awarding extra lives at a score threshold) that flow from the game's idea are often viewed as unprotectable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a mechanic is a functional necessity or a creative expressive choice. If a feature is intrinsic to implementing the underlying idea, courts may treat it as unprotectable scènes à faire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding monopoly over an idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright should not grant a monopoly over a broad idea or genre (e.g., all games about spaceships and asteroids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating protectability, consider whether recognizing protection for disputed elements would effectively prevent others from creating games in the same subject matter; courts seek to avoid overbroad protection that preempts ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admitted appropriation of idea does not equal infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An admission that a defendant "took plaintiff's idea" is insufficient by itself to establish copyright infringement if the defendant's remaining expression differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement analysis focuses on whether protected expression was copied. Defendants may concede borrowing the idea but prevail if their expressive choices differ sufficiently from the plaintiff's protected expression.
